translations.text: I have heard that the Hebrews lived in blessedness in Jerusalem, sharing out the gold-hoard and holding the kingship, as was their birthright. This was after victory had been given into Moses' hand through the Creator's might, along with a multitude of warriors, and they went out of Egypt in great strength. That was a brave people!
As long as they were allowed to rule that kingdom and govern its cities, they had shining wealth.
As long as that people were willing to keep their fathers' covenant with him, God was their shepherd, the Guardian of the heavenly kingdom, the holy Lord, the Ruler of glory.

The Creator of all things gave that host courage and might, so that with the protection of their army they often took the lives of many peoples who were not loyal to them. This went on until pride came over them at the wine-feast, with devilish deeds and drunken thoughts.
Then they abandoned [?] the skills of the law, the power of the Creator, though no one should turn the love of his spirit away from God.
Then I saw that company wander into error, the people of Israel doing wrong and committing sins. That was a grief to God!
Again and again the Guardian of the heavenly kingdom sent holy spirits to teach that people, and they offered wisdom to the host.

They believed in the truth of that wisdom for a little while, until a longing for earthly joys lured them away from eternal counsel, so that in the end they themselves abandoned the Lord's judgments and chose the devil's craft.
Then the Lord of the kingdom grew fierce of mind, hostile to the people to whom he had given possessions.
In the beginning he had guided those who at first, before that, had been dearest of mankind to the Creator, dearest of peoples, most beloved by the Lord; [?]
He showed the war-path to the high city to foreign warriors, into the homeland where Jerusalem stood, skilfully fortified and honoured with walls.

To the city of the prophet [?] the Chaldean people went onward, to the city where the possessions of the Israelites were, enclosed by fortifications. That host went there, a great and mighty troop, eager for evil.

The lord of men, the ruler of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, in his city stirred up deadly enmity out of malice, so that he began to work out in his mind how he could most easily overpower the men of Israel by the advance of hostile forces.
Then he gathered a bloodthirsty host from the south and from the north, and set out westward with an army of heathen kings toward the high city.
The guardians of Israel's homeland had love and the riches of life for as long as the Creator allowed them.
Then, I have heard, the race of old enemies easily [?] the wine-city of men. Those warriors did not believe; they robbed Solomon's temple, the glory of the halls, of red gold, of treasure and silver.
They plundered the treasures under the stone cliffs, all such as the noblemen were to possess, until they had broken down every one of the strongholds that stood as protection for the people.

They loaded up as booty the treasure of the hoard-guardians, wealth and ornaments, whatever was found there. Then they journeyed back with the possessions, and they also led the race of Israel on a long journey, on the eastern ways to Babylon: a countless number of men, heroes under the hand of heathen rulers.
Nebuchadnezzar forced the children of Israel, beyond all hope [?], the ones whom weapons had spared, into slavery as laborers.
Then he sent a great many of the thegns of his host westward, so that they would hold for him that people's land, a pleasant homeland, after the Hebrews were gone.
Then he ordered his reeves to search among the wretched remnant of Israel for those young men who were wisest in the teaching of the books that had been brought there.

He wanted the youths to learn a skill, so that they could tell him wisdom for his mind. This was not because he was able or willing to remember to thank God for the gifts that the Lord had granted him there for his prosperity.
Then they found there three noble youths, very wise and devout, young and good, of godly stock [?]. One was Hananiah, the second Azariah, and the third Mishael, chosen by the Creator.
Those three came before the king, steadfast and thoughtful, where the heathen sat, a king hungry for a great retinue, in the city of the Chaldeans.
When the Hebrew men had to show the proud one their wisdom in words, their high skill of mind, through their holy spirit, then the man, the ruler of Babylon, gave an order,
the strong-minded king commanded his thegns that the chief men must make sure, on pain of their lives, that the three young men lacked neither food nor clothing in their life in this world.
Then the ruler of Babylon was renowned, great and proud throughout the world, and terrible to the children of men. He did not keep the law, but lived in pride in every way.

Then, in his first sleep, after the mighty king had gone to rest, the terror of a dream came stirring into the mind of the people's leader. It showed how the world was wondrously ordered, not as people expect, until the new creation.
In his sleep the truth was revealed to him: that every kingdom must meet a cruel end, and the joys of earth must come to an end.
Then the wolf-hearted ruler of Babylon, who had gone to sleep drunk with wine, woke up. His mind was not glad; instead sorrow rose in him, the terror of the dream.
He could not remember what he had dreamed.
Then he called together those of his people who practised witchcraft most widely, and asked the gathering what had come to him in a dream while mortals lay at rest.
He had become terrified in that dread, since he knew neither the words nor the beginning of his dream; yet he ordered them to tell it to him.
Then the devil's prophets answered him unhappily (they had no judgement ready to tell the dream to the king):
"How can we, lord, work out things so hidden in your mind: what you dreamed, or what decree of fate wisdom revealed, if you cannot first relate its beginning?"
Then the savage-hearted king answered his wise men in displeasure:
"You were not as great as you told me, above all men in understanding, when you declared that you knew my life's fate, how it would turn out for me afterwards, or what I was to meet in the future."
"Now you do not know my dream, you who bring me wisdom before the company."
You will die, unless I learn the meaning of the true dream that my mind is calling to memory."
Then the multitude in that meeting place could not, through prophecy, think out or devise anything at all, since they were prevented from telling the king his dream,
the mysteries of fate, until the prophet Daniel came to judgement. He was chosen by the Lord, wise and righteous, to go into that hall.
He was the chief of the wretched remnant that had to obey the heathen.
God gave him a gift from heaven through the utterance of the Holy Spirit, so that an angel of God told him everything his liege lord had dreamed.

Then, when day dawned, Daniel went to interpret the dream for his lord. He wisely told him the destiny of peoples, so that the strong-minded king at once understood the beginning and the end of what had been shown to him.
Then Daniel had great glory and renown in Babylon among the scholars, after he told the king the dream. Because of his sins, the guardian of Babylon had earlier been unable to take it into his heart.

Yet Daniel could not bring it about that he would believe in the Creator's might. Instead, he began to make an idol on the plain that the bold-minded called Dura, which was in the nation of that name, mighty Babylon.

The guardian of that city, the ruler of the realm, set up an image for men against the Creator's will, an idol of gold, because he was not wise but cruel and without counsel. Right [?] then the men listened, when the sound of the trumpet's voice came over the citizens.

Then they knelt before the standard. The heathen people bowed down to the idol and worshipped the image. They knew no better counsel. They did wrong, as their lord did, steeped in sin and corrupted in mind.
The foreign nation, like their lord before them, committed folly and did wrong. (An evil reward came to them for it afterwards.)
There were three men of Israel in the prince's city who would never consent to their prince's decree and raise prayers to that sign, even though trumpets sounded there at the idol.
They were Abraham's children, good in their noble birth. They were steadfast in faith and knew the eternal Lord above, the Almighty.
The noble youths made it known that they would not take or keep that gold as their god, but only the high King, the shepherd of spirits, who had given them grace.

Moreover, they often boldly declared that they cared nothing for that idol. Nor could the heathen leader of the host force them by his might to that prayer, so that they, as men, would turn to the golden idol that he had appointed as his god.
Thanes told the prince that the captives [?] in this high city were of this mind: "They will not observe this, nor worship this idol that you wondrously made for your glory."
Then the guardian of Babylon, swollen with rage, answered angrily. He spoke grimly to the young men and declared harshly that they must pay worship at once or else suffer great affliction,
the terrible surge of fire, unless they, the Hebrew men, would seek protection from that most wicked thing, the gold that he had made his god.
Yet in their hearts the youths would not obey the heathen teachings.

They were earnestly resolved to fulfil all of God's law. They did not waver from the Lord of hosts, nor did they turn any further toward heathendom, nor did they seek safety through falsehood, though bitter death was threatened against them.
Then the stubborn king grew angry. He ordered a furnace to be heated to kill the youths, because they had rejected his powers.
When it had been heated as fiercely as he could with the dangerous flame of fire, he gathered the people there. The guardian of Babylon, grim and arrogant, ordered God's messengers to be bound.
Then he ordered his servants to thrust the boys, the young men, into the blaze of the fire.
The one who gave them help was ready. Though they forced them so cruelly into the embrace of the fire's flame, the mighty guardian of the Lord still saved their lives.
As many have heard, he granted them holy help there: God, the guardian of men, sent them the Holy Spirit from high heaven.
An angel came into the furnace, where they were suffering that torment, and sheltered the noble children in his embrace under the fiery roof.
Yet the surge of the flickering flame could not mar their beauty at all, because the Ruler saved them.
The heathen prince was fierce in mind and ordered them to be burned quickly.
The fire was kindled immeasurably great. Then the furnace was heated, the iron glowing all through. Many servants threw wood into it, as they had been ordered;

They carried brands into the burning of the bright fire (the wolf-hearted king wanted to set up a wall of iron around the devout ones), until the flame rose up over the beloved men and in its eagerness struck down far more than was fitting.

then the flame turned away from the holy ones onto the hateful men, the heathens. The youths were glad of heart. The servants burned outside around the furnace; the fire [?] turned to the harm of the malicious.
The lord of Babylon looked on at this. The Hebrew men were joyful. They eagerly praised the Lord in gladness and did as they knew how inside the furnace; their lives were saved.

The glad-hearted men worshipped God, under the protecting embrace of the one by whom the fierce heat of the fire was put to flight. The noble sons were let go by the flame's onrush, and it did them no harm there.
The roaring was no more grief to them than the shining of the sun, nor did the burning threaten the men who were in that peril. Instead the fire [?] went to those who had committed the guilt,
turned away from the holy youths onto the heathen captors, and it diminished the beauty of the accursed ones who had rejoiced at that deed.
Then the proud-minded king, when he trusted [?] his mind, saw a wonder come to pass in the torment; it seemed extraordinary to him.
The youths moved about unharmed in the hot furnace, all three devout ones. One more was there with them, in plain sight: an angel of the Almighty.
Nothing at all harmed them there in the furnace. Inside it was most like the time in summer when the sun shines, and the dew turns dry during the day, scattered by the wind.
It was the God of glory who saved them from that hostility.
Then Azarias, the holy one, spoke out of his inmost thoughts through the hot flame. Eager for good deeds, he acted, and praised the Lord, a man without sin, and spoke these words:
"Creator of all things, lo! You are strong in might to save men. Your name is glorious, beautiful and full of glory over the nations of men."
Your judgments are true every day, and mighty and victorious, just as you yourself are.
Your decrees concerning the world's riches are right and generous, ruler of the heavens.
Help us earnestly now, creator of spirits, and in your grace give help, holy Lord. Surrounded by flame, we now beg you for mercy because of afflictions, because of dire need, and in humility.
We brought this about while we lived in the world, and our ancestors also did wrong. In their pride the city-dwellers broke the commandments and scorned the way of holy life.

We are scattered across the wide earth, dispersed in crowds, without favour. Our life is despised and notorious in many lands, among many peoples, who have driven us into the power and possession of the worst of earthly kings,
into the captivity of the sword-fierce, and now we endure slavery to heathens. For this let there be thanks, King of glory of the hosts, that you appointed this punishment for us.

Do not abandon us, eternal Lord, for the sake of the mercies that men ascribe to you, and for the sake of the covenants that you, firm in glory, saviour from afflictions, Creator of spirits, made with Abraham and with Isaac and with Jacob.
You promised them by spoken word that in days of old you would increase their offspring, that after them it would be born in generations, and that the multitude would be great,

to be raised in station [?], like the stars of heaven that encircle the broad sky, or the sand of the sea-shores of the ocean-ways, which settles in the sea across the salt wave, so that its countless number would always grow through a multitude of years.
Fulfil now your original promise, even though few of them may be left alive!
Make your word and your glory shine in us!

Make known your skill and might, so that the Chaldeans and the many peoples who live as heathens under the heavens may learn of it, and learn that you alone are the eternal Lord, ruler of hosts and of the world's creatures, giver of victories, the true Creator!"
So the holy man was praising the Creator's mercy, and with his voice he recounted the abundance of God's might.
Then an all-bright angel was sent down from the heavens above, a man of beautiful appearance in his garment of glory. He came to them for comfort and to save their lives, with love and with kindness.

He thrust away the flame of the hot fire, holy and heaven-bright. Through his great might he swept away the gleam of the blaze and turned it aside, so that their bodies were not harmed at all. Instead, in anger, he struck the fire upon the enemies for their crimes.

Then, where the angel had arrived, it was breezy and pleasant in the furnace. It was most like the weather in summertime when a fall of raindrops is sent during the day, a warm shower from the clouds.
Just as the best of weather is, so it was in the fire through the Lord's power, as a help to the holy ones.

The hot flame was driven apart and quenched where the brave men walked through the furnace, and the angel with them, saving their lives. He was the fourth one there, with Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael.
There the three bold-minded men praised the Lord in their thoughts. The children of Israel called on all the creation of the earth to bless the eternal Lord, ruler of nations.
Then the three of them, wise in mind, spoke together with one voice: "Gentle Father, may the beauty of the world's crafted things and every one of your works bless you!
Heavens and angels, and the clear waters that dwell in glory above the skies in their rightful place in creation, may they honour you!

And may all creatures praise you, Almighty, each in its order: the heaven-bright stars that keep their courses, the sun and the moon, each one separately! And the stars of heaven, the dew and the precious shower, may they glorify you!
And may the spirits praise you, mighty God!
Burning fire and bright summer praise you, Savior! Night and day together, and every land, light and darkness, heat and cold together, praise you, each in its own order!
And may frosts and snows, bitter winter weather and the moving clouds praise you in the sky, mighty Lord! And may the lightnings, shining and swift as a flash, bless you!

The whole expanse of the earth, eternal Lord, the hills and the ground and the high mountains, the salt sea-waves, righteous Creator, the waves of the river current and the rising springs, the water-springs of the fountains: they honor you!
The whales praise you, and the birds of heaven that play in the air, and those that stir the ocean currents and the waters! And may the wild beasts and every kind of cattle bless your name!
And the children of men love you in their hearts, and Israel praises you, Creator of all possessions, in due order as their Lord!
And the powers of the hearts of the holy, the souls and spirits of each of the righteous, praise you, Lord of life, who give reward to all the humble, eternal Lord!
May Hananiah and Azariah and Mishael glorify you, Creator, with the thoughts of their hearts!
We bless you, Lord of every people, Father almighty, true Son of the Creator, Savior of souls, Helper of men, and you, Holy Spirit, we honor in glory, wise Lord!

We praise you, holy Lord, and glorify you with prayers! You are blessed and honored forever above the roof of the world, high King of heaven, with holy powers, light-giving Source of life, over every land!"
Then Nebuchadnezzar, the ruler of the nation, considered this with his closest companions:
"Many of you, my people, saw that we sent three men, commanded to the pyre, into the flame of the burning fire. Now I truly see four men there; my mind does not deceive me."
Then the king's counselor, wise and skilled in words, said: "What we look upon there with our eyes is a wonder.
Consider, my lord, what befits you!

Consider carefully who gave that gift to the young kinsmen! They praise God, the one eternal, and speak to him earnestly by every name of all things [?]. They thank him for his majesty with bold words, and say that he alone is almighty God, wise King of glory, of the world and of the heavens.
Summon those men out of the furnace, prince of the Chaldeans. It does no good at all for them to stay in that hateful place longer than you need them to."
Then the king ordered the young men to come to him.
The bold youths obeyed the command and turned back, noble in spirit, as they had been told; the young men went before the heathen king.
The bonds that had lain on their bones, the hateful device of the people's king, were burned away, and their bodies were saved.

Their beauty was not marred, nor was there any damage to their clothing, nor was their hair singed by fire. Instead, in the Lord's protection, the wise-minded men stepped gladly out of the grim terror, in the Spirit's favour.
Then the angel departed upward to seek eternal joys for himself on the high roof of the kingdom of heaven, a lofty thane, loyal to the holy Creator.
By that miracle he had honoured those who had earned it.

The youths praised the Lord before the heathen people. They taught him with true sayings and told him of many true signs, until he himself believed that the one who had rescued them from the darkness was the ruler of powers.
Then the bold guardian of Babylon, stern of mind, commanded his people that anyone who denied that the great Ruler of powers who had freed them from that slaughter was true should forfeit his life.
Then he gave back to them the remnant of their people who had been led there into the possession of their old enemies, so that they had honor.
Their glory was in Babylon after they had endured the burning. Their fame was made known among the nobility [?] after they had obeyed the Lord.
Their authority was mighty, after the Ruler of the heavens, the holy Guardian of heaven's kingdom, had shielded them against that harm.
Then, I have heard, after he perceived the wonder, the guardian of Babylon asked with true words how the three youths had come through the burning fire of the hot furnace, the sudden terror of fire.

God's messengers passed through the surging flame, so that the fierce hostility of the coals, of the perilous fire, did not harm them at all; instead the Lord's protection shielded their lives against the terror of that dread.
Then the lord began to hold a council. He called his people together, and at the assembly he proclaimed to the multitude what had happened and the wonder of God that had been shown in the young men:
"Consider now the holy might, the wise wonder of God! We have seen that he protected the young men, those who bore his praise, from death in the furnace, from the leaping flame;
for he alone is the eternal Lord, the almighty Judge, who gave glory and abundant success to those who bear his message.
Therefore he [?] reveals, through many a wonder, to the holy spirits who have chosen his favour.
It is known that Daniel told me the truth of a secret dream, which had long eluded the minds of many of my people, because the Almighty sent a mighty spirit, skills of wisdom, into his mind."
So spoke the leader of the host, the guardian of Babylon, after he perceived the sign, the clear token of God.

He did none the better for it. Pride harmed the prince: his mind grew loftier, and the thought in his heart grew greater in his spirit than was fitting, until the Almighty Creator forcibly set him lower, as he does to many of those who climb up through pride.
Then a dream was revealed to Nebuchadnezzar in his sleep; it came close to him.
It seemed to him that on the earth there stood, fair, a beautiful forest tree. It was firm in its roots and bright with fruit.
It was not like a grove; instead it towered up to the stars of heaven, as if it embraced the regions of the earth, the whole world, as far as the ocean streams, with its twigs and branches.
As he looked at it, it seemed to him that the forest tree sheltered wild beasts and alone held food for all of them. Birds also took their sustenance from the tree's fruit.

It seemed to him that an angel came descending from above, out of the heavens, and made a proclamation with his voice, in clear speech. He commanded that the tree be cut down and that the wild beasts flee away, and the birds as well, when its fall came.

Then he commanded that it be lopped of its own fruit, its twigs and branches. Yet there should still be a sign: the root of the forest tree should remain fast in the earth until green shoots come again, when God grants it.

He also commanded that the great tree be bound with fetters of brass and iron, and put bound into torment, so that its mind might know that one mightier than he wields punishment, and he cannot stand against him.
Then the earthly prince awoke from sleep (the dream was at an end). Fear of it came over him, terror from the spirit that God had sent there.

Then he commanded his people, the leaders of the nation, to gather together. The stern-minded king asked them all what the dream meant. This was not because he thought they knew it; he was testing how they would answer.
Then Daniel, God's messenger, was summoned to the judgment. A holy spirit from heaven had been given to him, and it strengthened his mind.
In him the Lord, the Guardian, knew a deep heart, broad thought, the skill of wisdom and wise speech. Often he revealed many a wonder, the powers of the Creator, before men.
Then the proud-hearted, heathen leader of the army began to tell of the terror of his dream, all the terror that had been shown to him.

He asked him to explain what the mystery meant, to lift up holy words and find in his mind how to say in true words what the tree that he had seen shining meant, and to foretell for him the course of what was fated.
Then he kept silent. Yet Daniel, at that judgment, perceived the truth: that his lord, the ruler of men, was guilty against God.
The wise man hesitated, yet he spoke in words to the prince, a messenger skilled in the law:
"Guardian of the host, it is no small wonder that you saw in a dream a tree as high as heaven, and heard the holy words, angry and terrible,
which the angel spoke: that the tree, which had stood firm before, should have its branches cut off and fall forward, and then be without joy among the wild beasts,
dwell in the wilderness, and that its root should be left in the earth and stay still in its place for a set time, as the voice said, and after seven seasons receive seed again.

So your glory will lie fallen. As the tree grew high to the heavens, so you alone are guardian and guide for men, for all earth-dwellers. You have no adversary, no man on earth, except the Creator alone.

He will cut you off from the kingship and send you friendless into exile. Then he will turn your heart, so that you will not remember the joys of human company, nor know any understanding except the ways of wild beasts. Instead, you will live a long time and dwell throughout the forest, leaping like the harts.

You will have no mealtime food except the grass of the moor, nor any settled place of rest. Instead, showers of rain will wake you and drive you about like the wild beasts, until after seven winters you truly believe that there is one Lord for all men, ruler and mighty one, who is in the heavens.
Yet it pleases me that the root remained still in its place, as the voice said, and that after seven seasons it would receive seed.
So your kingdom will remain at rest, your sole power among men, until you come back.
My lord, think on firm counsel.
Give alms, be a shelter for the poor, intercede before the Lord, before the time comes when he casts you out of your earthly kingdom.
Often the Lord allows many nations to make amends, when they themselves are willing, and to fast for their sins, before God's sudden attack ends their lives through dreadful terror."

However many true words Daniel spoke to his lord through the power of wisdom, the mighty one, guardian of the world, would never heed them. Instead his mind rose up, high from the heart, and he paid harshly for it.
Then the king of the Chaldeans began to speak with great boasting, when in his glory he saw the city-work, the city of Babylon, encircling the broad plain of Shinar and towering high:

[?] what the war-leader had made for his troop through great wonder. Then he became arrogant above all men, overbearing in his heart, because of the special gift that God had given him: the kingdom of men, the world to rule over in the life of men.
"You are the great city, my famous city, which I built for my honour, a spacious kingdom. In you I will rest; I will possess you as my dwelling and homeland."
Then for that boast the lord of men was seized, and he went into flight, alone in his pride above all men.

So, in days of misery, Nebuchadnezzar went the most grievous journey of all men who afterward came back alive to their people, in God's punishment, after God's enmity, wrath from heaven, hostility had struck him.
For seven years together the king of the city of wine suffered torment in the wilderness of wild beasts.
Then the man of hardship, the companion of wild beasts, looked up through the passing of the clouds.

Then he remembered in his mind that the Lord, the high king of the heavens, was for the children of men the one eternal Spirit. Then he turned back again from his mad mind, where he had before widely borne the spirit of a war-crazed man close to his heart.
Then his spirit returned to remembrance of God, and his mind to men, after he recognized the Lord.

Then the wretched one set out to journey back, the naked exile, enduring hostility, a wondrous outcast without clothing, humbler in his thoughts, to mankind, than he had been when he was guardian of men in his boasting.
The world stood waiting for its lord, the land and homeland for the prince, seven years together, so that the kingdom under the heavens did not diminish until the ruler came.
Then the guardian of Babylon was set again in rulership. He had better ways and a brighter faith in the Source of life: that God gave every man prosperity or punishment, just as he himself wished.

Then the prince of the people no longer put off the words of the prophets. Instead, wherever he had the power to speak, he proclaimed far and wide the might of the Lord. He told his people of his journey, the far wandering he had gone through among the wild beasts, until a wise mind from the Lord God came into his spirit, when he looked up to the heavens.

Fate had come to pass, the wonder had been made known, the dream proved true, the torment endured, the judgment given, just as Daniel had said before: that the leader of the people would meet hard journeys because of his pride.
So he eagerly preached the powers of the Lord to mankind, after Daniel had for a long while taught judgments to the city-dwellers in Babylon.

After the companion of beasts, the refugee among wild creatures, Nebuchadnezzar, came back from his wandering, from his harsh punishments, he afterward guarded the wide kingdom and held the treasure of men and the high city, wise,
the very mighty ruler of peoples, king of the Chaldeans, until death struck him. So no man on earth was his adversary until God wished to take the high kingdom from him through his fall.
Afterward his descendants dispensed riches there, wealth, twisted gold, in that wide city, the sanctuary of nobles, generously, the great power of the hoard, when their lord lay dead.
Then his third generation rose up in that nation.
Belshazzar was lord of the cities and ruled the kingdom of men until pride harmed him, hateful arrogance. Then came the last day on which the Chaldeans held the kingship.
Then after a little while the Lord granted rulership to the Medes and Persians, and let the glory of Babylon dwindle, which those men should have kept.
He knew the nobles who were supposed to rule the kingdom to be in wrongdoing.

Then the lord of the Medes, sitting at home, resolved on what no one had attempted before: that he would break into Babylon, the sanctuary of nobles, where princes dispensed wealth under the shelter of the walls.
Of fortresses that was the best known to the peoples, the greatest and most famous of those that men inhabited, Babylon among cities, until Belshazzar provoked God through fierce boasting.

They sat at wine, enclosed by the wall, and did not at all fear the hostility of warriors, though a people of enemies came marching in armed array to that high city so that they might break into Babylon.
Then on the last day the king of the Chaldeans sat at the feast with his kinsmen, where the leader of the host became drunk with mead.

He commanded the treasures of Israel to be brought to the nobles, the holy sacrificial vessels, into the hands of the men, which the Chaldeans, warriors in the city, had earlier taken entirely by royal might, the gold in Jerusalem,
when they destroyed the glory of Judah with the edges of swords and, coming with clamour, took bright ornaments as plunder. When they plundered the temple, Solomon's hall, they boasted greatly.
Then the lord of the cities grew glad of mind and boasted fiercely in defiance of God. He said that his armies were greater and mightier as a protection for men than the eternal Lord of Israel.

A sign came to him where he gazed, terrible before the nobles inside the hall, because he had spoken lying words before the people. There, to their terror, the angel of the Lord let his hand come into the high hall, and on the wall it wrote mysterious words in crimson letters for the city-dwellers.
Then the leader of the people grew afraid in his mind, terrified by that dread. He saw an angel's hand in the hall writing the punishment of Shinar.
Many crowds of men, warriors in the hall, talked about what the hand had written as a sign to the people of the city.
Crowds of men came to see that wonder.
Then they searched hard in the thoughts of their hearts for what the hand of the Holy Spirit had written.
Men skilled in mysteries, men of noble race, could not read the angel's written message until Daniel, chosen by the Lord, wise and righteous, came walking into that hall.

Great power from God was in his spirit. I have heard that the guardians of the city eagerly tried to buy him with gifts, so that he would read and explain the letters to them and say what the mystery meant.

The one strong in the law, God's messenger, wise in thought, answered him: "I do not carry the Lord's judgments to the people for payments of money, nor do I [?] seek any gain from you. Instead I tell you your fate for no payment, the mystery of the words, which you cannot turn aside.
Out of arrogance you have taken the holy vessels of the sacrifice as your own property, into the hands of your men.
From these you began to drink to devils, these vessels that the Israelites once kept at God's ark as their law required, until boasting deceived them, a wine-drunk mind, as shall happen to you.
Your forefather would never carry God's golden vessels about in boasting. He did not exult any more for it, even though his army brought the treasure of the Israelites under his power.
Instead, the ruler of nations more often said truthfully before his host, after the Guardian of glory had shown him wonders, that He alone was Lord and Ruler of all creation,
who had given him dominion and the unblemished glory of an earthly kingdom. And now you deny that He is living, He who rules in His might over devils."
